title: How One Ion Carries Different Messages

scenes.tts: The first film showed how moving calcium creates a cytosolic rise. How can that same ion trigger different responses? A cell cannot label one calcium ion for contraction and another for secretion. Instead, it controls where the rise happens, and when and how often.

scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: calcium teal; ER purple; channels gold; pumps coral; buffers blue; sensors green; active output orange; traces white. One teal dot reaches two differently placed green sensors. Question marks grow above both while the cell fills the frame.

scenes.visual: The question marks transform into the title: How One Ion Carries Different Messages. Keep the cell, ER, gold channel, and both sensors visible behind the brief title.

scenes.tts: Open one gold channel. Calcium is highest near its pore before buffers capture and pumps remove it. The teal plume fades with distance. A sensor anchored beside the channel samples that local domain. An identical sensor across the cytosol meets much less free calcium.

scenes.visual: Zoom into one gold channel. Teal dots form a large bright plume beside the pore and thin across the frame. Blue buffer blobs capture drifting dots. Two identical green sensors remain near and far. Label plume and concentration bars schematic.

scenes.tts: Predict before either sensor changes. Both sensors switch on only above the same calcium threshold. The channel opens briefly. Which sensor responds: the one beside the pore, the one across the cell, or both? Follow the fading plume.

scenes.visual: Hold the near and far green sensors at equal size. A gold channel opens and a teal schematic plume begins but stops short of both sensors. Place one question above them and keep gentle calcium motion. Show one dashed line labelled THRESHOLD (schematic, same for both sensors).

scenes.visual: Continue slow teal drift within the frozen schematic plume. Neither sensor activates; the question remains centered.

scenes.tts: Only the nearby sensor responds. Calcium beside the pore crosses the threshold; the lower level far away does not. The near sensor binds calcium, changes shape and exposes an orange output surface. Location has selected a reader without changing the calcium or the reader's binding properties.

scenes.visual: Complete the teal plume to the near sensor only. That green two-lobed cartoon takes up teal ions; its two lobes swing open and one orange output tab appears. A dashed threshold line on a schematic bar beside each sensor: the near bar crosses it, the far bar stays below. The far identical sensor stays unchanged and neutral. Do not draw any molecular structure.

scenes.tts: A local event can also recruit more release. Calcium from one site may help open a neighbouring release channel. Then the next site can recruit another. The moving front becomes a wave, and many sensors across the cell can respond. This spreading route is positive feedback.

scenes.visual: Zoom back to the full purple ER. Three gold release channels open sequentially as a teal front reaches each one. Green sensors activate behind the front. Label the moving teal band schematic and POSITIVE FEEDBACK.
scenes.narration: A local event can also recruit more release. Calcium from one site may help open a neighbouring release channel. Then the next site can recruit another. The moving front becomes a wave, and many sensors across the cell can respond. This spreading route is positive feedback.

scenes.tts: Now transform distance into time. One sensor sees isolated calcium spikes, each followed by full recovery. Another sees closely spaced spikes. Both trains can contain similar individual rises, yet their intervals differ. A reader with a slowly fading active state can distinguish those intervals.

scenes.visual: The ER wave straightens into a horizontal time axis. Draw two schematic trains of identical calcium pulses: widely spaced above, closely spaced below. Green reader bars beside each trace fade continuously between pulses; label them 'schematic reader activity'.
scenes.narration: Now transform distance into time. One sensor sees isolated calcium spikes, each followed by full recovery. Another sees closely spaced spikes. Both trains can contain similar individual rises, yet their intervals differ. A reader with a slowly fading active state can distinguish those intervals.

scenes.tts: With long gaps, the reader returns toward rest before the next spike. Close spikes arrive while some activity remains. The responses can build. Calcium has not acquired a new identity. Timing matters because the reader keeps a biochemical memory that outlasts each brief rise.

scenes.visual: Continue the schematic traces. The upper green memory bar falls to baseline between pulses. The lower bar accumulates into a taller orange activity bar. Label the bars 'schematic reader activity'; no numbers appear.
scenes.narration: With long gaps, the reader returns toward rest before the next spike. Close spikes arrive while some activity remains. The responses can build. Calcium has not acquired a new identity. Timing matters because the reader keeps a biochemical memory that outlasts each brief rise.

scenes.tts: Cells give calcium meaning by controlling where and when free calcium rises. The size of a rise matters too; this film concentrates on place and timing. Local domains favour nearby readers. Coordinated release can spread the response. Repeated spikes favour readers that retain activity between rises. Cells combine these patterns with different sensors; there is no universal decoder.

scenes.tts: The cell therefore writes information without changing the ion itself. Channel position sets the starting place. Feedback can enlarge the territory. Opening and closing set the rhythm. Sensors read only the calcium pattern that reaches them, on the time scale their own chemistry can remember.
